screens.title: What is a Vulnerability Scanner?
screens.narratorSegment: A vulnerability scanner is an automated tool that inspects systems, services, and applications for known security weaknesses by comparing observed behaviors and configurations against a database of known issues. Scanners surface missing patches, default credentials, open services, and common application flaws tied to CVEs or vendor advisories. They are immensely useful because they can quickly test thousands of IPs or application endpoints and provide structured reports. A concrete example: a scanner queries a web server and identifies an outdated library version that matches a documented CVE, returning severity and remediation suggestions. But it's important to understand limits: scanners focus on known issues and pattern matches, so they can miss zero-day flaws or logic errors unique to a custom app. A common misconception is treating every flag as a confirmed breach; many findings are potential issues that need human validation. To validate, an ethical hacker cross-checks version strings, inspects configs, and, when permitted, performs controlled, non-destructive verification attempts. Takeaway: scanners accelerate discovery, but human analysis determines whether a finding is exploitable and how to prioritize it. Which flagged finding would you validate first in a critical system and why?

keyIdea.title: Scanner core claim
keyIdea.text: Automated detection of known vulnerabilities accelerates assessments but requires human verification for real-world context and exploitability.

content.html:
Core Concept › Vulnerability Scanner
Definition
An automated tool that compares responses and configurations to known vulnerability databases and generates prioritized findings.
Capabilities
  • Detects missing patches, default credentials, and open services.
  • Reports CVE references and suggested remediation steps.
  • Supports credentialed scans for deeper visibility.
Limitations
  • Primarily finds known vulnerabilities, misses zero-days and custom logic flaws.
  • Can generate false positives and false negatives requiring manual validation.
Key Takeaway

Use scanners to cover breadth quickly; use manual testing to confirm depth and exploitability.

Concrete example
A scanner reports Apache version X with CVE-XXXX-XXXX and suggests updating. You verify the server version and whether the vendor patched it or if backported fixes negate the reported vulnerability.
Misconception
Not every reported vulnerability is exploitable—assume findings are hypotheses that need verification, not final diagnoses.
Pro tip
When a scanner flags a version issue, cross-check with configuration files or vendor notes to detect backported patches that remove the vulnerability.

screens.title: Common Scanners: Nessus, OpenVAS, Web Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Ethical hackers commonly combine multiple scanners to achieve broader coverage. Nessus is a widely-used proprietary scanner known for an extensive plugin database and frequent updates; it excels at broad network and host checks and supports credentialed scanning for deep inspection. OpenVAS, now part of the Greenbone Vulnerability Management suite, is an open-source alternative with a daily-updated NVT feed and a web interface for managing tasks and reports. For web applications specifically, Burp Suite Professional and Acunetix offer richer interactive testing and custom payloads for S Q L injection, XSS, and CSRF. A practical example: use OpenVAS or Nessus for initial network-wide discovery to identify outdated services, then run Burp Suite to probe application logic and validate web-specific findings. A frequent misconception is assuming one tool is sufficient. Each tool has blind spots: network scanners can miss complex web logic, and web tools might not check host configurations. When planning an engagement, choose tools that complement each other and match the target scope. Takeaway question: which combinations would you use for a mixed environment of servers, databases, and web apps? Common Scanners: Nessus, OpenVAS, Web Tools means combine scanners that complement each other: network/host scanners for breadth, web tools for application depth; avoid single-tool reliance.. In practical terms, strengths, coverage, and typical use-cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison › Tool strengths
Nessus vs OpenVAS vs Web Tools
Choose based on coverage needs: network, host, or web application depth.
Nessus (proprietary)
Extensive plugin database and frequent updates. Strong for credentialed host scanning and commercial support.
OpenVAS / GVM (open-source)
Daily NVT feed, web UI, good for network/host scanning in open environments and lab practice.
Burp Suite / Acunetix (web)
Interactive and scriptable testing for web logic, custom payloads, and catching complex application flaws.
When to combine
Start with a broad network scan, then use web tools for application-specific checks and manual validation for critical items.
Example workflow

Use OpenVAS to discover open services and outdated software, then run Burp Suite against the web front-end to validate and exploit web-specific vulnerabilities safely in a lab.

Quick note
No single scanner covers every class of vulnerability. Plan a complementary toolset that matches the environment you are testing.

Process › OpenVAS setup
Key commands (lab)
Update feeds, start services, then access the web UI to continue configuration.
# Update GVM feeds (NVTs, SCAP, CERT)
sudo gvm-feed-update

# Start GVM services (if not already running)
sudo gvm-start

# Access the web interface at https://127.0.0.1:9392
# Change default credentials immediately after first login
Notes
Feed updates may take time; wait for NVT synchronization. Ensure your lab VM has internet access or preloaded feeds for offline setups.
Checklist before scanning
  • Confirm NVT feed synchronization and recent update timestamp.
  • Start GVM/OpenVAS services and verify no errors in service logs.
  • Reset default admin credentials and use secure passwords.
  • Test web UI login at the configured address and port.
Common mistake

Rushing to scan before feeds finish syncing leads to outdated results and missed CVEs. Always confirm feed update completion.

screens.title: Creating Targets and Tasks in GVM
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a proper target and scan task in GVM is an essential repeatable step in vulnerability scanning. Start by defining a named target and listing the host IP address or range and an appropriate port list. Use the 'All IANA assigned TCP and UDP' port list for broad discovery or a narrower list when scope requires. Next create a scan task, selecting a scan configuration such as 'Full and fast' for comprehensive checks or 'Discovery' for a lightweight initial pass. Associate the previously created target with the task, confirm the scanner selection, and save. Finally, start the task and monitor progress until completion. A concrete example: create a target named Vulnerable_VM with host 192.168.1.100, then create a task named Basic Scan - Vulnerable VM using 'Full and fast', select the target and start it. A misconception is treating task defaults as optimal; always review and adjust settings for scope and safety. Takeaway: define clear targets and conservative defaults for initial scans, then iterate with more aggressive checks if permitted. screens.title: Credentialed vs Non-credentialed Scans
screens.narratorSegment: Credentialed scans use valid login credentials so the scanner can authenticate into the target and inspect configuration, installed packages, and patch status. This deeper view typically yields more accurate results and fewer false positives because the scanner can read version files and settings directly. Non-credentialed scans run without credentials and simulate an external attacker's perspective, which is useful for assessing exposure from the outside but often misses internal configuration issues. A concrete example: a credentialed scan on a Linux host can verify installed package versions and detect a missing security patch, while a non-credentialed scan might only infer package versions from banner data and generate ambiguous results. A common misconception is that credentialed scans are always safe to run at full aggressiveness; they still require cautious configuration because authenticated checks may exercise services differently and could impact target stability. Takeaway: use non-credentialed scans to map external exposure, then credentialed scans to validate and reduce false positives when you are authorized to do so. Credentialed vs Non-credentialed Scans means credentialed scans provide more accurate internal visibility; non-credentialed scans show the external attacker perspective—use both when permitted.. In practical terms, when to use credentials and how depth of visibility changes findings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition › Credentialed vs Non-credentialed
Credentialed scans
Authenticated checks that can read config files and package versions for higher accuracy.
Benefits
  • Deeper visibility into installed software and missing patches.
  • Lower rate of false positives for version-related findings.
Caution
Authenticated checks can act differently and should be run with conservative settings on fragile systems.
Non-credentialed scans
Unauthenticated scans that simulate an external attacker and may miss internal configuration issues.
Benefits
  • Show exposure visible to the network or internet.
  • Safer initial pass on unknown or production systems.
Misconception
Assuming a non-credentialed scan that reports nothing means the system is secure; it may only mean internal issues are hidden without authentication.

screens.title: Interpreting Scan Reports and CVE References
screens.narratorSegment: Interpreting a vulnerability report requires understanding severity labels and CVE context and then relating those to business impact. Reports typically categorize findings as Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Info and include CVE IDs for documented vulnerabilities. A concrete example: a finding labeled Critical with a CVE reference signals a known exploit or severe impact; your next step is to validate that the target is truly affected and to assess potential impact on business operations. Use CVE details to learn exploitability and vendor-provided remediation. Prioritize vulnerabilities using CVSS score and the asset's role—an exploitable medium-severity flaw on a public-facing database can outrank a higher-scored issue on an isolated test server. A common misconception is treating severity labels as absolute; they are a starting point for triage, not the final priority list. Takeaway: combine report severity, CVE exploitability details, and real-world asset criticality to prioritize remediation and validation steps. screens.title: False Positives and False Negatives
screens.narratorSegment: False positives occur when a scanner reports a vulnerability that is not actually present or exploitable in the target's specific configuration. A textbook example from the chapter: a scanner reports Apache 2.2. x vulnerable to a CVE while the server actually runs Apache 2.4. x or has the patch backported, making the finding incorrect. False negatives are more dangerous: they are real vulnerabilities the scanner fails to detect, often because the issue is new, custom, or requires logic-aware testing. To handle false positives, perform targeted manual checks such as confirming the running version, inspecting patch history, or testing non-destructively where permitted. For false negatives, rely on complementary tools and targeted manual testing of custom applications. A common misconception is assuming scanners are infallible; acceptance of scanner output without validation is risky. Takeaway: always document validation steps and update scan configurations or credentials when false positives reveal configuration blind spots. screens.title: Risks of Automated Scanning and Safe Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Automated scans can be noisy and, in some cases, disruptive. Scanners send many probes that may trigger intrusion detection or prevention systems and produce alerts. In fragile environments, aggressive scan settings can overload services and even cause denial-of-service conditions. To avoid harm, always obtain written authorization that defines scope and allowed timing. Start with non-intrusive or discovery scans, run during off-peak windows, and gradually increase intensity if needed and permitted. A concrete scenario: scanning legacy systems with default aggressive timing might cause service failures; instead, use lower parallelism and fewer simultaneous checks. Another common mistake is running credentialed scans with default aggressive checks on production databases; authenticated checks can exercise database queries that increase load. Takeaway: plan scans with safety limits, monitor system health during the scan, and have a rollback or pause plan if adverse effects appear. screens.title: Effective Scanning Strategy and Prioritization
screens.narratorSegment: An effective scanning strategy starts with defined scope and written authorization. Decide which assets are in-scope and which scan profiles are appropriate. Schedule scans during off-peak hours to reduce operational risk and prefer discovery scans before full scans. Prioritization should combine scanner severity, CVE exploitability, and the asset's business importance. For example, a medium-severity issue on a public database may warrant higher priority than a high-severity issue on an isolated development host. After identifying critical findings, validate them manually: confirm versions, reproduce the symptom non-destructively, and, if permitted, attempt controlled exploitation to confirm impact. Always record validation steps and rationale for triage decisions so remediation teams have clear guidance. A common misconception is assuming all critical findings must be patched immediately without considering backups, maintenance windows, and compensating controls. Takeaway: align scanning cadence and prioritization with business risk and operational readiness to make remediation efficient and safe. screens.title: Hands-on Lab: Basic OpenVAS Scan Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through a basic OpenVAS (GVM) scan against a deliberately vulnerable VM. Begin by ensuring your GVM instance has updated NVT feeds and running services. Use the feed update command and start services as needed. Next, open the GVM web interface and log in with secure credentials. Create a target named Vulnerable_VM with host 192.168.1.100 and a broad port list. Then create a task named Basic Scan - Vulnerable VM, select 'Full and fast' or start with 'Discovery' if you prefer a lighter initial run, and associate the target. Start the task and monitor progress until complete. Once the report is ready, filter results by severity and list the top three critical or high findings with CVE IDs. For each top finding, perform manual validation: confirm version strings, check for backported patches, and document whether the finding is a true positive, false positive, or requires deeper testing. A common mistake is not changing default credentials—secure the admin account before exposing the interface. Takeaway: follow a repeatable checklist: update feeds, secure credentials, define targets, run safe scans, and validate critical results before reporting.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how automated vulnerability scanners speed discovery, how to choose the right tool, and how to interpret results responsibly. Scanners like Nessus and OpenVAS compare system responses to known vulnerability databases, surfacing missing patches, misconfigurations, and common application flaws. That speed is invaluable, but a report is not a verdict. You will learn to validate findings, distinguish false positives and false negatives, and follow a cautious scanning strategy to avoid service disruption. We will also walk through a basic OpenVAS setup and a hands-on scan against a deliberately vulnerable machine so you can see the workflow end-to-end. By the end of the chapter you will be able to configure a scan, read a report with CVE and severity context, and prioritize remediation using business impact. Remember: scanners are powerful assistants, not replacements for human judgment. As you start, ask yourself which findings you would manually validate first and why.

In this chapter you will build practical skills for automated vulnerability assessment and responsible scanning. First, you will learn to identify and categorize widely used scanners like Nessus and OpenVAS, recognizing each tool's role and typical use cases. Second, you will configure and execute a basic OpenVAS scan, update feeds, and understand the significance of credentialed versus non-credentialed scans. Third, you will interpret scan reports: read severity labels, locate CVE references, and learn methods to distinguish false positives from true positives using manual validation techniques. Fourth, you will adopt a safe scanning strategy: obtain written authorization, select appropriate scan profiles, schedule off-peak runs, and validate critical findings before remediation. Each objective ties to practical steps and a verification milestone so you can demonstrate competency during an engagement. Learning Objectives means run, interpret, and use vulnerability scans responsibly while avoiding common mistakes like relying solely on automated output.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This second objectives screen describes measurable outcomes and why they matter. You will demonstrate configuring OpenVAS: updating NVT feeds, starting GVM services, creating a target, and running a scan against a lab VM. You'll interpret a generated report by identifying the top critical or high findings, reading CVE IDs, and assessing remediation suggestions. You will practice distinguishing false positives by checking version and configuration details and learn a simple manual verification approach for high-severity items. Finally, you will develop a scanning strategy that includes written authorization, scoped targets, non-intrusive defaults, scheduling during off-peak periods, and manual validation steps for critical findings. These outcomes map directly to responsible, professional conduct during an ethical hacking engagement. A vulnerability scanner is an automated tool that inspects systems, services, and applications for known security weaknesses by comparing observed behaviors and configurations against a database of known issues. Scanners surface missing patches, default credentials, open services, and common application flaws tied to CVEs or vendor advisories. They are immensely useful because they can quickly test thousands of IPs or application endpoints and provide structured reports. A concrete example: a scanner queries a web server and identifies an outdated library version that matches a documented CVE, returning severity and remediation suggestions. But it's important to understand limits: scanners focus on known issues and pattern matches, so they can miss zero-day flaws or logic errors unique to a custom app. A common misconception is treating every flag as a confirmed breach; many findings are potential issues that need human validation. To validate, an ethical hacker cross-checks version strings, inspects configs, and, when permitted, performs controlled, non-destructive verification attempts. Takeaway: scanners accelerate discovery, but human analysis determines whether a finding is exploitable and how to prioritize it. Which flagged finding would you validate first in a critical system and why?

Ethical hackers commonly combine multiple scanners to achieve broader coverage. Nessus is a widely-used proprietary scanner known for an extensive plugin database and frequent updates; it excels at broad network and host checks and supports credentialed scanning for deep inspection. OpenVAS, now part of the Greenbone Vulnerability Management suite, is an open-source alternative with a daily-updated NVT feed and a web interface for managing tasks and reports. For web applications specifically, Burp Suite Professional and Acunetix offer richer interactive testing and custom payloads for S Q L injection, XSS, and CSRF. A practical example: use OpenVAS or Nessus for initial network-wide discovery to identify outdated services, then run Burp Suite to probe application logic and validate web-specific findings. A frequent misconception is assuming one tool is sufficient. Each tool has blind spots: network scanners can miss complex web logic, and web tools might not check host configurations. When planning an engagement, choose tools that complement each other and match the target scope. Takeaway question: which combinations would you use for a mixed environment of servers, databases, and web apps? Common Scanners: Nessus, OpenVAS, Web Tools means combine scanners that complement each other: network/host scanners for breadth, web tools for application depth; avoid single-tool reliance.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Setting up OpenVAS as part of Greenbone Vulnerability Management starts with updating its vulnerability feeds and ensuring services are running. In many lab distributions you run a feed update command to pull NVTs, SCAP, and CERT data so the scanner recognizes recent CVEs. For example, the provided commands update feeds then start GVM services. After services are running, you access the web interface at your instance address and change any default credentials to secure the interface. A concrete example: run the feed update, then the start command, and confirm the web UI is reachable at the documented port. A common misconception is that a fresh install is ready immediately; often feeds must synchronize and initial tasks like certificate generation take time. Also avoid running these operations against production systems without authorization. Takeaway: verify feeds are current, services are healthy, and credentials are secured before scanning. Creating a proper target and scan task in GVM is an essential repeatable step in vulnerability scanning. Start by defining a named target and listing the host IP address or range and an appropriate port list. Use the 'All IANA assigned TCP and UDP' port list for broad discovery or a narrower list when scope requires. Next create a scan task, selecting a scan configuration such as 'Full and fast' for comprehensive checks or 'Discovery' for a lightweight initial pass. Associate the previously created target with the task, confirm the scanner selection, and save. Finally, start the task and monitor progress until completion. A concrete example: create a target named Vulnerable_VM with host 192.168.1.100, then create a task named Basic Scan - Vulnerable VM using 'Full and fast', select the target and start it. A misconception is treating task defaults as optimal; always review and adjust settings for scope and safety. Takeaway: define clear targets and conservative defaults for initial scans, then iterate with more aggressive checks if permitted. Creating Targets and Tasks in GVM means name and scope targets clearly, choose an appropriate scan config, and monitor tasks—start light, escalate only when permitted.. In practical terms, step-by-step task creation and launch workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Credentialed scans use valid login credentials so the scanner can authenticate into the target and inspect configuration, installed packages, and patch status. This deeper view typically yields more accurate results and fewer false positives because the scanner can read version files and settings directly. Non-credentialed scans run without credentials and simulate an external attacker's perspective, which is useful for assessing exposure from the outside but often misses internal configuration issues. A concrete example: a credentialed scan on a Linux host can verify installed package versions and detect a missing security patch, while a non-credentialed scan might only infer package versions from banner data and generate ambiguous results. A common misconception is that credentialed scans are always safe to run at full aggressiveness; they still require cautious configuration because authenticated checks may exercise services differently and could impact target stability. Takeaway: use non-credentialed scans to map external exposure, then credentialed scans to validate and reduce false positives when you are authorized to do so. Credentialed vs Non-credentialed Scans means credentialed scans provide more accurate internal visibility; non-credentialed scans show the external attacker perspective—use both when permitted.. In practical terms, when to use credentials and how depth of visibility changes findings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Interpreting a vulnerability report requires understanding severity labels and CVE context and then relating those to business impact. Reports typically categorize findings as Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Info and include CVE IDs for documented vulnerabilities. A concrete example: a finding labeled Critical with a CVE reference signals a known exploit or severe impact; your next step is to validate that the target is truly affected and to assess potential impact on business operations. False positives occur when a scanner reports a vulnerability that is not actually present or exploitable in the target's specific configuration. A textbook example from the chapter: a scanner reports Apache 2.2. x vulnerable to a CVE while the server actually runs Apache 2.4. x or has the patch backported, making the finding incorrect. False negatives are more dangerous: they are real vulnerabilities the scanner fails to detect, often because the issue is new, custom, or requires logic-aware testing. To handle false positives, perform targeted manual checks such as confirming the running version, inspecting patch history, or testing non-destructively where permitted. For false negatives, rely on complementary tools and targeted manual testing of custom applications. A common misconception is assuming scanners are infallible; acceptance of scanner output without validation is risky. Takeaway: always document validation steps and update scan configurations or credentials when false positives reveal configuration blind spots. Automated scans can be noisy and, in some cases, disruptive. Scanners send many probes that may trigger intrusion detection or prevention systems and produce alerts. In fragile environments, aggressive scan settings can overload services and even cause denial-of-service conditions. To avoid harm, always obtain written authorization that defines scope and allowed timing. Start with non-intrusive or discovery scans, run during off-peak windows, and gradually increase intensity if needed and permitted.
